cues.text: Week one asks one question: why do we turn text into numbers at all?
Because a model can only compute with numbers. It cannot read the word good.
So every method in this course is a way of turning text into numbers, and each one keeps something and loses something.
For every method, ask three things: what problem does it fix, what goes in and comes out, and where does it still fail.
Step one is tokenization: split the text into tokens. A token can be a word, a piece of a word, or punctuation.
Don't becomes do plus n apostrophe t.
A word-level vocabulary has a problem: a word it never saw in training is out of vocabulary.
Subword tokenizers fix this. Unhappiness is split into pieces the model already knows.
B P E merges the most frequent pairs and is used by G P T. WordPiece marks continuation pieces with two hashes and is used by BERT.
Now give each word a column. One-hot: a vector as long as the vocabulary, with a single one.
Bag of words adds them up: it counts how often each word appears.
But it forgets the order. Dog bites man and man bites dog get exactly the same vector.
N-grams bring back some local order: New York becomes one feature, and not good becomes one feature.
Counts treat every word the same. TF-IDF down-weights words that appear everywhere.
I D F is the log of N over d f. N is the number of documents, d f is how many documents contain the word.
Four reviews. Good appears in two of them, so its I D F is log of four over two, about zero point six nine.
Movie appears in all four. Log of four over four is zero: it does not tell the documents apart.
The weight is count times I D F. Good twice in one review gives about one point three nine. It is a weight, not a sentiment and not a probability.
One-hot vectors are all equally far apart. Cat is as far from dog as from car.
Dense embeddings give each word fifty to three hundred learned numbers, so similar meanings land close together.
The famous example: king minus man plus woman lands near queen.
Word2Vec and GloVe are static: bank gets one vector, whether it is a river bank or a bank loan.
Contextual models like BERT give each occurrence its own vector, built from the words around it.
Last idea: when is a large language model the wrong tool?
For a spam filter, the lecture compared an L L M with Naive Bayes. The accuracy gap was small: ninety-nine point two versus ninety-eight point five percent.
But the L L M costs about thirty thousand dollars a month, and Naive Bayes under ten. It takes a hundred to a thousand milliseconds, Naive Bayes under ten.
Add privacy, interpretability and hallucinations. Don't use a bulldozer to crack a chestnut: start with a cheap baseline.
